strengths: Practically significant systems contribution: a 3.4x end-to-end training speedup over the original 3DGS implementation (and 1.4x over a TamingGS-integrated baseline) while preserving rendering quality, demonstrated on two GPUs (A100, RTX3090).

Well-motivated analysis: the paper grounds its design decisions in detailed GPU profiling, including warp-state sampling (Fig. 3, Table 1), L2 cache hit-rate degradation over training (Fig. 4), and per-function execution-time breakdowns (Fig. 2). This diagnostic evidence is more rigorous than typical for systems papers in this area.

The individual techniques (cluster culling with AABBs, cluster compaction, Morton-code layout, tighter 2D AABBs, 8x8 tiles, multibatch gradient reduction avoiding atomicAdd contention) are each supported by targeted micro-evaluations (Figs. 5-7), showing e.g. ~40% reduction in rendered patches and large fragment-count reductions.
Genuinely useful observation that TamingGS's reported speedup is largely attributable to a fused Adam optimizer rather than sparsity itself — a clarification of value to the community.

Dual API (scripted with autograd + CUDA extension) is a sensible usability contribution for research prototyping versus production, and the codebase is claimed to be open-sourced, aiding reproducibility and downstream adoption.
weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to a single dataset (Mip-NeRF 360, 9 scenes). No Tanks&Temples, Deep Blending, or large-scale scenes; generalization of the speedup and quality claims is not established.

No proper component-wise ablation table quantifying each technique's contribution to the end-to-end 3.4x speedup. Figures 5-7 show intermediate metrics (L2 hit rate, patch/fragment counts) but not per-technique runtime gains, making it hard to attribute improvements.
The abstract claims ~30% GPU memory reduction, but no memory measurements or table are provided anywhere in the paper.

No quantitative comparison with gsplat [22], the most directly competing modular library; Figure 1 positions LiteGS as superior without supporting numbers, which weakens the usability/modularity claim.

Fairness of the quality comparison (Table 3) is questionable: the authors 'applied specific processing and parameter adjustments to the SfM step' for 3DGS, making baseline metrics incomparable to published results and raising concerns about configuration parity; details of these adjustments are not given.

Presentation is below the bar for a camera-ready paper: Figure 1's caption is a placeholder ('Figure 1: ....'), the code URL is missing in Section 4, inconsistent capitalization/titles ('Modular Designed', 'cluster culling&compacting'), and grammar issues throughout. This suggests an unfinished manuscript.

Novelty is modest: most techniques are assemblies of known ideas (Morton codes [15], cluster culling from real-time rendering [1], stream compaction [17], sparse gradients from TamingGS [13]). The contribution is primarily integration and engineering, which is acceptable for an Applied/Systems paper, but the paper would be stronger if positioned explicitly as such with correspondingly thorough system evaluation.
Missing discussion of limitations (e.g., re-blocking cost from Morton reordering, behavior on very large scenes, dependency of gains on GPU architecture) and no societal-impact or broader discussion.

strengths: Well-motivated systems contribution: the paper identifies concrete, measured bottlenecks in the original 3DGS implementation (backward rasterization dominance, atomicAdd contention, declining L2 hit rates, warp divergence) using credible profiling evidence (Figs. 2-4, Table 1), which is a solid diagnostic foundation for the proposed optimizations.

The collection of techniques (Morton-code clustering with block size 128, cluster-level culling and compacting, tighter 2D AABBs with an 8x8 tile size, multibatch reduction with shared-memory gradient compaction) forms a coherent end-to-end design, and the reported speedups are substantial: 3.4x over 3DGS and 1.4x over a TamingGS-integrated baseline on two GPUs (A100, RTX3090), across all nine Mip-NeRF 360 scenes.

The analysis in Sec. 4.4 attributing Taming-GS's sparse-Adam speedup primarily to PyTorch's multitenor/fused Adam interface rather than sparsity itself is a genuinely useful and honest insight for practitioners.

The dual API design (scripted PyTorch ops with autograd for prototyping plus a CUDA path for production) addresses a real usability gap in the 3DGS ecosystem and increases the potential impact of the framework.
Quality is reported alongside speed (SSIM/PSNR/LPIPS in Table 3), showing the acceleration does not meaningfully degrade reconstruction quality.
weaknesses: The abstract and introduction prominently claim a ~30% reduction in GPU memory usage, but no memory measurements are reported anywhere in the paper. This key quantitative claim is unsupported and must be substantiated with per-scene memory tables.

There is no component-wise ablation. The method stacks at least five distinct techniques (clustering/compacting, cluster culling, tighter AABB, 8x8 tiles, multibatch reduction, fused Adam), yet the paper never quantifies each component's individual contribution to the 3.4x speedup. As an Applied/Systems contribution, this per-component evidence is central to the scientific case, and its absence is a serious gap.

Evaluation is limited to a single dataset (Mip-NeRF 360, 9 indoor/outdoor scenes). No results on Tanks&Temples, Deep Blending, or large-scale scenes, and no rendering-speed (FPS) results despite the framework targeting 'performance-critical applications'. Generalization of the speedup claims is therefore not established.

The comparison to gsplat (the closest prior modular library, acknowledged in Related Works and Fig. 1 as the main competitor on the speed-modularity axis) is absent from the experiments. The evaluation only compares against the original 3DGS and a TamingGS-patched variant; without gsplat baselines the claimed advantage of LiteGS's modular design is not demonstrated empirically.

The quality comparison in Table 3 is confounded: the authors state they applied 'specific processing and parameter adjustments to the SfM step' yielding COLMAP results better than the original paper's. Reporting metrics only against their own modified 3DGS baseline, without the standard published numbers or an unmodified-baseline comparison, makes the quality equivalence claim hard to verify.

The manuscript is not camera-ready in presentation: Figure 1's caption is a placeholder ('Figure 1: ...'), the code URL in Sec. 4 is literally blank ('available at .'), there are numerous typos and inconsistent capitalization ('clustering', 'cluster culling&compacting', 'Torch CUDA Extension'), and the claimed source-code availability cannot be checked, weakening reproducibility.

Novelty of individual components is limited: Morton-code ordering, cluster-based culling with AABs, compaction, and tighter bounding volumes are adapted from prior work (TamingGS, DistWAR, standard GPU practice), and the paper is candid about this. The main novelty is integration and engineering, which would be acceptable for a systems paper if the evaluation were more thorough.

Some design choices are under-justified: the changed density-control schedule (fewer, larger point-management operations) may alter the optimization trajectory, but its effect on quality/convergence is not isolated; the 8x8 tile size analysis relies on fragment counts (Fig. 7) rather than end-to-end timing breakdowns separating binning overhead from rasterization gains.

strengths: Well-motivated systems work with genuine diagnostic depth: the profiling analysis of backward-pass bottlenecks (warp cycles per issued instruction, MIO/LG throttle analysis, L2 cache hit-rate degradation over training) goes beyond superficial motivation and clearly explains *why* the original 3DGS implementation is slow.

The proposed techniques (Morton-code clustering for spatial locality, cluster-level culling with compaction, tighter 2D AABBs, multi-batch shared-memory reduction replacing AtomicAdd) are coherently tied to the identified bottlenecks, and each is supported by targeted measurements (Figs. 5-7).

Substantial and reproducible results: 3.4x speedup over original 3DGS and 1.4x over the TamingGS-integrated baseline on two different GPUs (A100 and RTX3090), across all Mip-NeRF 360 scenes, with essentially unchanged quality metrics.
The analysis in Sec. 4.4 attributing TamingGS's sparse-Adam speedup primarily to fused rather than sparse kernels is an insightful correction that benefits the community.

The dual-API modular design (script-level with autograd for prototyping, CUDA extension for production) is a sensible and useful engineering contribution; source code availability supports reproducibility.
Appropriate for evaluation as an Applied/Systems contribution: value lies in the integration, profiling, and engineering rather than a new algorithm, and the work delivers clearly on that.
weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to a single dataset (Mip-NeRF 360 indoor/outdoor scenes). No Tanks&Temples, Deep Blending, or higher-resolution/forward-facing results, so generality of the speedup and quality preservation claims is not established.
The abstract claims a ~30% reduction in GPU memory usage, but no memory measurements are reported anywhere in the paper. This headline claim is currently unsupported.

The quality comparison (Table 3) is confounded: the authors modified the SfM/COLMAP step for Mip-NeRF 360, so their 3DGS baseline numbers differ from the original paper. The comparison is thus against a re-tuned baseline on a modified data pipeline, and per-scene deltas (e.g., bicycle PSNR -0.10, flowers PSNR +0.53) are small and hard to interpret without variance or additional seeds.

The 8x8 tile size change alters the rasterization granularity of the original method; its effect on quality and on generalization to other scenes is not isolated, and there is no end-to-end ablation table attributing the 3.4x speedup to individual components (cluster/compact, AABB, tile size, multibatch reduction).

No direct comparison with gsplat, the most closely related modular library (acknowledged in Fig. 1 and Sec. 2), despite it being the natural baseline for the usability and speed claims; the speed axis in Fig. 1 is anecdotal rather than measured.

Presentation is rough: Figure 1's caption is a literal placeholder ('...'), section titles are grammatically awkward ('Modular Designed', 'clustering'), and there are typos ('simpling', 'the simpling result'). The paper is quite short, and some method descriptions (e.g., how re-blocking is amortized over density control) are under-specified, weakening reproducibility.
No discussion of limitations (e.g., dependence on NVIDIA warp/scheduler behavior, applicability to other GPU architectures) or societal impact.

strengths: The paper presents a coherent system-and-algorithm co-design that addresses the 3DGS training bottleneck at three well-motivated levels (GPU rasterization, data management, densification algorithm), and the layered analysis of why existing pipelines underutilize the GPU (atomic-add conflicts, poor spatial locality) is insightful and well argued.

The warp-based rasterizer with the scanline Gaussian formulation and strategic mixed-precision is a genuinely novel and effective design: Table 3 shows 7-13x speedup over the atomic rasterizer, ~4x over per-splat parallelization, and ~1.5x over recent Tensor-Core methods, at all primitive scales.

Results are strong and extensive across three standard benchmarks (MipNeRF-360, Tanks & Temples, Deep Blending), evaluated at three parameter scales (turbo/balance/quality). The claims of 13.4x speedup over 3DGS with comparable quality and matching 3DGS-MCMC quality with <1/2 parameters and ~10x speedup are credible and Pareto-dominant in Table 1.

Ablations are meaningful and targeted: the Cluster-Cull-Compact ablation (Table 2), operator-level rasterizer comparison with reasonable experimental controls (Table 3), and component-wise densification ablation (Table 4) each isolate a module's contribution, addressing the concern that end-to-end speedups conflate effects.

The opacity gradient variance densification metric is a conceptually clean improvement over the ambiguous position-gradient heuristic, and its near-zero computational cost is enabled by the underlying rasterizer — a good example of the claimed synergy between system and algorithm layers. The framework is open-sourced, supporting reproducibility. Appropriately attributed prior art (DISTWAR, Taming 3DGS, TC-GS, cluster-cull-compaction in rendering) is cited throughout.
weaknesses: All experiments are run on a single GPU (RTX 3090). Several design choices (warp size 32, register counts, FP16 vs BF16 throughput, tile size 4x32=128) are explicitly hardware-tuned, so the reported speedups may not transfer cleanly to other GPUs; results on at least one additional GPU architecture (e.g., Ada or Blackwell) would substantially strengthen the claim of a general framework.

There are internal inconsistencies in the reported numbers: Table 4's full-model MipNeRF-360 PSNR is 28.12, whereas Table 1's LiteGS-quality reports 28.25 (and the table caption's parenthetical numbers differ again), making it unclear which configuration the densification ablation uses. Similarly, Table 2's 'w/o culling' PSNR (28.28) is slightly higher than 'w/ culling' (28.25) but the text describes this as a trade-off that should be discussed more precisely.

No qualitative visual comparisons (rendered images, zoomed crops, or geometric quality figures) are provided anywhere in the paper; given that LPIPS results in the lightweight setting are admittedly worse than Mini-Splatting v2, visual evidence of where quality is gained or lost is needed.

The FP16 mixed-precision choices (half-precision transmittance, half2-packed gradients, integer-warp-reduce mantissa accumulation) could plausibly affect training stability and final quality, but the paper does not provide a precision ablation or any numerical-accuracy analysis of the custom exponent-alignment reduction.

Only average training times are reported without variance over repeated runs, and the rasterizer benchmark (Table 3) uses only the 'garden' scene; timing claims at the sub-minute scale are sensitive to measurement noise. The hyperparameter sensitivity of the new densification scheme (5-epoch densification interval, 10-epoch decay, 80% schedule) is not explored.

Presentation quality is uneven: several typos ('Gausians', 'signle', 'raterization', 'Cluter-Cull-Compact', 'PSRN'), the contribution bullet points and abstract repeat identical claims, and the limitations discussion is confined to a short future-work paragraph. The contribution is best characterized as Applied/Systems rather than Algorithms/General; under that lens the empirical evidence is appropriate, but the paper should state this framing and temper 'new SOTA benchmark' language that leans on quality metrics where comparisons with SSS (40K iterations) are not fully controlled.

strengths: The paper makes a convincing systems-level contribution: by attacking the 3DGS training bottleneck at three coordinated layers (warp-based rasterization, Morton-coded Cluster-Cull-Compact data management, and a new densification criterion), it achieves order-of-magnitude speedups (up to 13.4x vs. original 3DGS) while maintaining or improving quality, which is a substantial and practically important result for the community.

The warp-based rasterizer with the scanline Gaussian formulation and mixed-precision warp-reduction tricks is a genuinely novel low-level design, and Table 3 provides operator-level benchmarks against four rasterization backends (atomic, per-splat, tensor-core, warp-based), which fairly isolates the rasterizer contribution rather than relying only on end-to-end timings.

The opacity-gradient-variance densification metric is well-motivated: the argument that low-variance signals unconvergence while high-variance signals true under-reconstruction is intuitive and is supported by a dedicated ablation (Table 4) against both hard-reset and error-based alternatives, showing 0.3-0.6 dB gains.

Evaluation covers three standard benchmarks (MipNeRF-360, Tanks&Temples, Deep Blending), compares against a broad set of recent SOTA baselines (3DGS-MCMC, TamingGS, Mini-Splatting v2, SSS), and includes ablations for each of the three components. The framework is stated to be open-sourced, supporting reproducibility.

The claimed Pareto-dominance across parameter scales (turbo/balance/quality configurations) is a useful framing, and the finding that LiteGS matches 3DGS-MCMC quality with less than half the parameters and ~10x speedup is a meaningful advance.
weaknesses: Only aggregated results over dataset suites are reported; per-scene results are absent, and no rendering speed (FPS), memory measurements beyond qualitative claims, or qualitative visual comparisons are provided. For a paper whose central claim is training efficiency and quality, the omission of per-scene breakdowns and render-time figures weakens the completeness of the evidence.

There are inconsistencies in the reported numbers: Table 1 lists LiteGS-quality on Mip-NeRF 360 at 28.25 dB PSNR, while Table 4 lists the full model at 28.12 dB; the footnote in Table 1 about '0.780/24.72/0.133 in 30K iterations takes 398s' is confusingly worded and hard to reconcile with Table 2. These discrepancies need clarification and suggest the results were compiled from different configurations without careful cross-checking.

All experiments are on a single RTX 3090; the heavy reliance on hardware-specific tuning (4x32 tile size matching NVIDIA register counts, FP16 SIMD throughput, warp-reduce instructions) raises questions about generalization to other GPU architectures, and the claims about RTX 5090 performance are speculative.

The mixed-precision strategy (FP16 for transmittance, alpha, and gradient packing; integer-mantissa warp reduction for covariance gradients) could introduce numerical error accumulation over 30K iterations, but no analysis or experiment quantifies precision-related degradation or edge cases (e.g., very low transmittance regimes).

Several relevant recent acceleration baselines (e.g., Speedy-Splat, EDC-style split strategies, FlashGS) are discussed in related work but not compared against in experiments, and the '1.4x speedup over SOTA lightweight models' claim rests on a comparison with only Mini-Splatting v2.

The paper is framed as Algorithms/General (though arguably Applied/Systems), and under that framing the algorithmic novelty is concentrated in the variance-based densification criterion; the rasterization and data-management components, while effective, are adaptations of established ideas (warp reductions, scanline rasterization, Morton-order clustering from prior work), which somewhat reduces conceptual novelty even though the integration and engineering are strong.

The densification strategy introduces several coupled hyperparameters (5-epoch densification interval, 10-epoch opacity decay over the first 80% of training) whose sensitivity is not explored, limiting insight into robustness across scene types.

strengths: Strong, well-motivated system-and-algorithm codesign: the paper identifies concrete bottlenecks at three levels (GPU rasterization, data layout, densification) and addresses each with a targeted technique (warp-based raster, Cluster-Cull-Compact via Morton sorting, opacity-gradient-variance densification with opacity decay), rather than a collection of ad-hoc tricks.

Substantial and convincing empirical results: up to 13.4x speedup over original 3DGS at comparable quality, 1.4x over Mini-Splatting v2 in the lightweight regime, and new quality/SOTA trade-off points versus 3DGS-MCMC and SSS, evaluated across three standard benchmarks (MipNeRF-360, Tanks & Temples, Deep Blending) with PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS.

Good ablation studies: Table 3 isolates rasterizer performance against atomic, per-splat, and tensor-core baselines at multiple primitive counts; Tables 2 and 4 separately quantify the Cluster-Cull-Compact pipeline and both densification components (decay, variance metric). The experimental design for ablations is thoughtful (e.g., operator-level timing to avoid confounds from differing primitive counts).

The opacity gradient variance densification criterion is a conceptually clean and novel contribution: the low-variance (unconverged) vs. high-variance (true under-reconstruction) distinction directly addresses the known ambiguity of the original ADC, and it is enabled cheaply by the underlying rasterizer — a genuine synergy between system and algorithm layers.
The framework is open-sourced, which supports reproducibility and practical impact for the 3DGS community.
The claim structure is honest in places: the paper acknowledges slightly worse LPIPS than Mini-Splatting v2 and footnotes iteration-count differences for the SSS comparison.
weaknesses: Experiments are confined to a single GPU (RTX 3090). Several techniques are explicitly hardware-dependent (tile size 4x32 chosen to match register count, warp-reduce instructions on Ampere+), so generality of the speedup across architectures (e.g., Ada, Blackwell, consumer vs. datacenter, or mobile GPUs) is not demonstrated. The claim of 'possibly second-level on RTX 5090' is speculative and unsupported.

Some fairness concerns in comparisons: LiteGS-quality uses 30K iterations while several baselines (SSS, 3DGS-MCMC) use 40K, and LiteGS adopts TamingGS learning rates and its own densification hyperparameters rather than matched schedules. Although the paper footnotes the SSS comparison and reports a 40K-equivalent figure, a controlled iteration-matched comparison across all baselines would strengthen the headline SOTA claims.

Mixed-precision design choices are justified qualitatively but not validated numerically. Using FP16 for transmittance T (an iteratively multiplied quantity that can underflow) and the integer-mantissa warp-reduce for covariance gradients could introduce accuracy loss; no precision-error analysis or quality comparison against full FP32 is provided.

Presentation has enough rough edges to hamper reproducibility: Algorithm 1 leaves quad = -0.5d with 'd' undefined and the scanline formulation is not fully derived; several typos ('Cluter', 'signle', 'donated' for 'denoted', 'PSRN', 'raterization'); the densification metric formula (Ci x Var = Si - Mi^2/Ci) is stated but the actual thresholding rule and full hyperparameter list are under-specified. Contribution type is effectively Applied/Systems rather than Algorithms/General; this is fine, but the paper should frame claims accordingly (systems contribution with an algorithmic component), which slightly tempers the weight given to the novel-metric claim.

No variance reporting: single runs per configuration, no standard deviations over seeds, and the sensitivity of results to the chosen densification/decay intervals (5/10 epochs, 80% of training) is not explored even though these hyperparameters were evidently tuned.

The abstract/intro phrase 'sets a new accuracy record' overstates: per Table 1's own footnote, SSS at 40K iterations still leads on Tanks & Temples in some metrics; claims should be softened to 'state-of-the-art trade-off'.

Missing related work on faster 3DGS training kernels is largely covered, but discussions of GPU memory usage / peak memory are mentioned qualitatively without measurements; there is also no discussion of societal impact, which for an efficiency framework is a minor omission but worth noting.
